tokyo_umezono_asakusa_honten.price_note: ⚠ PRICES ARE 本体価格 — BEFORE TAX. The shop prints them that way throughout, so add roughly 10% at the till; that is unusual in this dataset and worth flagging. Several items are listed by the shop with no price at all and carry an empty one here rather than an invented figure. ⚠ WHY A KANMIDOKORO IS WORTH READING CAREFULLY: traditional Japanese sweets are one of the very few categories where the DEFAULT is naturally gluten-free and plant-based — agar, adzuki, black sugar syrup, glutinous rice, kudzu and millet are the building blocks, and dairy and egg simply are not part of the tradition. Founded 1854. But the exceptions are sharp and they are not obvious from the names: the どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば are wheat, and ⚠⚠ THE くず餅 IS THE TRAP — a Kanto 久寿餅 is made from FERMENTED WHEAT STARCH, not from kudzu at all, despite what the name says. That is the single most misleading item in Japanese confectionery for a coeliac and this shop is in Asakusa, squarely in Kanto. Ask specifically.

items.en: The house speciality since 1854 — half-pounded and kneaded millet, steamed, served with slow-simmered koshian
items.note: ⚠ THE FIND ON THIS MENU, AND THE SHOP EXPLAINS IT ITSELF. The name says あわ (foxtail millet) and the shop states the grain is actually 餅きび — PROSO MILLET — half-pounded, kneaded and steamed, then paired with koshian. Both are millets and NEITHER IS WHEAT: millet is naturally gluten-free, and adzuki with sugar is plant-only. So the ingredients of this dish, as the shop describes them, reach both diets — a 170-year-old recipe the shop says is unchanged since 安政元年. Recorded as ask rather than gf because no allergen statement is made and this is the only source for the composition. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

Shiruko is adzuki beans, sugar and water, normally with a piece of 餅 — glutinous RICE — in it. No wheat and nothing animal in the traditional build. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

寒天 is AGAR, set from seaweed — not gelatin and not wheat — so it is plant-based and gluten-free by nature. 黒蜜 is black sugar syrup and あんこ is adzuki beans with sugar. This combination is one of the few traditional Japanese dessert families that suits both diets on its ingredients alone. Anmitsu is agar cubes, adzuki, fruit and kuromitsu, usually with 求肥 (glutinous rice) too. Takeaway version ¥650. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

This combination is one of the few traditional Japanese dessert families that suits both diets on its ingredients alone. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

This combination is one of the few traditional Japanese dessert families that suits both diets on its ingredients alone. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

No price published. 白玉 is glutinous RICE flour — no wheat. 寒天 is AGAR, set from seaweed — not gelatin and not wheat — so it is plant-based and gluten-free by nature. 黒蜜 is black sugar syrup and あんこ is adzuki beans with sugar. items.en: Mitsumame — agar, peas, fruit and syrup
items.note: No price published. As mamekan with fruit added. 寒天 is AGAR, set from seaweed — not gelatin and not wheat — so it is plant-based and gluten-free by nature. 黒蜜 is black sugar syrup and あんこ is adzuki beans with sugar. This combination is one of the few traditional Japanese dessert families that suits both diets on its ingredients alone.

No price published. Tokoroten is 天草 seaweed set into noodles — a NOODLE with no grain in it at all, which makes it one of the few things called a noodle in this dataset that a coeliac can consider. The catch is the dressing: Kanto tokoroten is normally served with 三杯酢, which contains SOY SAUCE. Ask for it with kuromitsu, the Kansai way, or plain.

⚠⚠ THE TRAP, AND IT IS THE WORST-NAMED ITEM IN JAPANESE CONFECTIONERY. A Kanto 久寿餅 is NOT made from kudzu: it is made from FERMENTED WHEAT STARCH, left to ferment for a year or more, and it is a Tokyo speciality precisely in the Asakusa and Kawasaki area where this shop stands. The name, the texture and the kinako-and-kuromitsu service all read exactly like the kudzu version, which IS gluten-free. Assume wheat here and ask before believing otherwise. Plant-based either way.

No price published. The mochi is rice, but zoni is a savoury soup: the broth is dashi — bonito — normally seasoned with soy sauce, so it is a wheat route and a vegan one at once, and the only savoury item on this board.

No price published. 茶そば is nearly always a WHEAT-and-buckwheat blend — the matcha weakens the dough, so the wheat proportion tends to be higher than in plain soba, not lower. The tsuyu is soy and dashi.

Glutinous RICE flour around adzuki, with whole beans in the skin — no wheat and nothing animal in the traditional build. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

Glutinous rice with yomogi (mugwort) and adzuki — despite 草 in the name there is no wheat in the traditional recipe. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

Namagashi are normally 練り切り — white bean paste with 求肥 or 山芋 — with no wheat. Designs change with the season and the recipe with them, so ask on the day. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

Contents change and are not published. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

The pancakes either side of the bean paste are WHEAT FLOUR, and dorayaki batter contains EGG and honey — so this one is out on both axes while the filling would have suited both. Chestnut version ¥350. Gift boxes of 6, 8 and 10.
No price published. A moulded sponge cake — wheat flour and egg — around adzuki.

Marked 休止 (suspended) by the shop. Recorded anyway because the answer is instructive: kintsuba is a block of adzuki jelly given a thin WHEAT-FLOUR batter skin on each face. The filling is the whole dish and the coating is the problem.
The shop's named confection, sold in gift sets with the ningyoyaki. Not described anywhere on the site; 虎 sweets of this kind are normally a baked sponge, which would be wheat and egg. Ask.

No unit price published; sold in boxes of 8, 12 and 16. Yokan is adzuki, sugar and AGAR set into a block — no wheat, no dairy, no egg. Structurally one of the safest traditional sweets there is. Standing caveat for every item here: this is a kanmidokoro that also bakes どら焼, 人形焼 and きんつば, so there is wheat flour in the building and no allergen statement anywhere.

items.ja: 桜餅・道明寺（季節限定）
items.note: No price published. Worth knowing that the two names are two different sweets: 道明寺 (the Kansai style) is coarsely ground GLUTINOUS RICE, while the Kanto 長命寺 style is a thin crêpe of WHEAT flour. This shop lists 道明寺 by name, which is the rice one. Wrapped in a salted cherry leaf.

items.ja: 柏餅（こし・つぶ・みそ）
items.en: Kashiwamochi — smooth bean, chunky bean or miso, seasonal
items.note: No price published. Rice mochi wrapped in an oak leaf. The みそ filling adds a question the other two do not: miso is frequently 麦味噌, BARLEY, which is not on Japan's statutory allergen list.

No price published. Unlike the くず餅 above, a くず饅頭 genuinely is made with KUDZU starch — a translucent dome of kudzu around bean paste, and kudzu is a root starch with no gluten. Two items on one menu with 葛 in the name and opposite answers, which is exactly why the くず餅 note matters. Ask to confirm real kudzu rather than a potato-starch substitute; either way it is not wheat.
No price published. Glutinous rice rolled in adzuki, kinako (roasted SOYBEAN flour) or sesame — all plant, none wheat.

items.en: Red and white manju for celebrations
items.note: No price published. A standard 紅白まんじゅう is a steamed WHEAT-flour bun around bean paste — the one celebration item where the wrapper is the problem. Plant-based otherwise.
No price published. A large ceremonial mochi — glutinous rice and nothing else in the traditional form.

tokyo_bangkok_cosmo_shokudo.price_note: ⚠ TAX STATUS UNKNOWN: Tabelog prints its own warning on this listing — 「税込金額か不明の価格です。正確な価格は店舗へ直接ご確認ください」 — it does not know whether these figures include tax. That is the third shop in this dataset carrying that warning, so the numbers below could be up to 10% higher at the till. ⚠ THE USEFUL THING ABOUT THIS MENU IS THAT THE SHOP NAMES ITS OWN STARCHES, which almost none do. It calls its noodles 米麺 — RICE noodles — in the descriptions of パットシーユー and レックナーム, and it states that its カノムトゥアイ is made with 米粉, RICE FLOUR. Both are naturally gluten-free and said by the kitchen rather than inferred. Against that it also names the exceptions: パットマーマー is fried INSTANT NOODLES, which are wheat, and it describes the パットウンセン as タイ醤油味 — Thai SOY SAUCE — in so many words. So this is a menu where reading the shop's own descriptions actually answers the question, which is rare. Structurally the food is rice-and-coconut based and the dessert list is the strongest in the shard for a vegan.

items.ja: ポッピアソット / 生春巻き
items.en: Fresh spring rolls — the shop calls them chewy and packed with vegetables
items.note: FRESH spring rolls are wrapped in RICE paper, not the wheat sheet a fried roll uses. Filling and dipping sauce undeclared, and the dip is where both diets turn.

items.ja: カノムパンナークン / 海老パン 2ピース
items.en: Prawn toast, two pieces — the shop's most popular starter; prawn paste spread thickly on bread and fried
items.note: The shop's own description names the bread: prawn paste spread on パン and deep-fried. Wheat bread, fried. Four pieces ¥780.

items.ja: トートマンクン / 海老のすり身揚げ
items.en: Fried prawn cakes, made one by one and served straight from the fryer
items.note: Battered and deep-fried: wheat coating, shared oil. Prawn surimi is commonly bound with wheat starch as well.

items.ja: トートマンプラー / 魚のすり身揚げ
items.en: Thai fish cakes with herbs worked through — the shop calls them Thai satsuma-age
items.note: Battered and deep-fried: wheat coating, shared oil. The shop's own comparison to さつま揚げ is apt: Japanese fish cake is commonly bound with WHEAT STARCH.

items.ja: カイチアオムーサップ / 豚ひき肉入り玉子焼き
items.en: Thai omelette with minced pork — the shop calls it a gentle home dish
items.note: A Thai omelette is egg fried in hot oil, usually seasoned with fish sauce — no wheat in the classic build. Egg and pork.

items.ja: ムーデッドディアオ / 豚の千切り揚げ
items.en: Sun-dried fried pork — the shop suggests trying its distinctive seasoning
items.note: Sun-dried marinated pork, fried without batter in the classic form; the marinade normally includes fish sauce and often soy.

items.ja: カオキャップクン / タイえびせんべい
items.note: Thai prawn crackers are usually tapioca starch and prawn, wheat-free in the classic form; the recipe is not stated.

items.ja: ヤムメットマムアン / タイミニおつまみナッツ
items.en: Cashews scattered with salt and spring onion
items.note: Nuts, salt and spring onion — the simplest thing on the board and one of the few outright vegan items. Seasoned nut mixes sometimes carry a soy coating.

items.ja: ナンガイトード / 鶏皮揚げ
items.note: Battered and deep-fried: wheat coating, shared oil.

items.ja: ヤムトウミョー / 豚挽肉と豆苗サラダ
items.en: Pea shoot and minced pork salad with a house dressing
items.note: A lime-and-chilli dressing with no wheat route; fish sauce is the vegan problem.

items.ja: ソムタム / 青パパイヤのサラダ
items.note: Shredded raw papaya, chilli and lime — no wheat in the dish, a strong coeliac prospect. Dressed with fish sauce and usually dried shrimp.

items.ja: ヤムウンセン / 春雨サラダ
items.note: 春雨 glass noodles are MUNG BEAN or potato starch, not wheat. Dressed with fish sauce and lime, normally with minced pork and dried shrimp.

items.ja: ヤムムータクライ / 豚挽肉とレモングラスのレタス包みサラダ
items.en: Minced pork and lemongrass wrapped in lettuce
items.note: Wrapped in LETTUCE rather than any pancake or wrapper, which is the good news. The dressing is fish-sauce based.

items.ja: ラープガイ / イサーン地方の鶏挽肉サラダ
items.en: Isaan minced chicken salad, hot and sour
items.note: Larb is minced meat, herbs, lime and toasted RICE powder — the thickener is rice, not flour. Fish sauce. Pork version ¥900.

items.ja: ヤムプラーサムンプライ / 揚げ白身魚とタイハーブの健康サラダ
items.en: Fried sea bass with Thai herbs
items.note: The fish is fried before it is dressed. Battered and deep-fried: wheat coating, shared oil.

items.ja: ヤムマーマー / タイ即席めんサラダ
items.en: Thai instant noodle salad — the shop invites you to try the new sensation
items.note: マーマー is Thailand's instant noodle brand and instant noodles are WHEAT. A salad that reads fresh and is built on a wheat noodle.

items.ja: ヤムアボガド / タイ式アボガドサラダ
items.en: Thai-style avocado salad with a sharp dressing
items.note: Avocado and a lime dressing — the closest thing here to a vegan salad, and fish sauce is the standard dressing. Ask.

items.ja: プラークン / 海老のタイハーブサラダ
items.note: Lime and chilli with fish sauce.

items.ja: サイウア / チェンマイ・ソーセージ
items.en: Chiang Mai sausage — packed with kaffir lime leaf, herbs and spice
items.note: Sai ua is pork with lemongrass, galangal and curry paste — no wheat in the classic build, unlike a Japanese sausage which is commonly bulked with wheat rusk. Seasoning undeclared.

items.ja: ネームスライス / 北部名産酸味ソーセージ
items.note: Naem is pork fermented with garlic and RICE — the rice drives the fermentation, so no wheat in the classic build.

items.ja: サイクロークイサーン / タイ東北地方のもち米入りソーセージ（5本）
items.en: Isaan sausage with glutinous rice, five pieces
items.note: Named for its filling: pork fermented with GLUTINOUS RICE. "Glutinous" describes the sticky rice and contains no gluten — this is a rice sausage, not a wheat one.

items.ja: ガイヤーン / 屋台式・鶏の炙り焼き
items.note: Marinated in coriander root, garlic, pepper and fish sauce, then grilled dry — one of the better prospects here. Marinades sometimes include soy.

items.ja: コームヤーン / 豚の炙り焼き
items.note: Grilled; the nam jim jaew dip is fish-sauce based and marinades often use soy.

items.ja: プーニムポンカリー / ソフトシェルクラブのカレー炒め
items.en: Soft-shell crab in curry powder — the shop's number one stir-fry, generously portioned
items.note: Soft-shell crab is floured and fried before it enters the sauce, and pad pong curry normally includes oyster sauce and evaporated milk. Egg.

items.ja: パックブンファイデーン / 空芯菜炒め
items.note: The closest thing to a plant main and it still needs a conversation: pak boong is stir-fried with fermented soybean and oyster sauce, plus fish sauce. Ask whether garlic and chilli alone is possible.

items.ja: タレーナンプリックパオ / シーフードのチリオイル炒め
items.note: Nam prik pao is a roasted chilli jam built on dried shrimp and fish sauce, and the stir-fry adds oyster and soy sauce.

items.ja: チューチークン / 海老のレッドカレー炒め
items.note: A coconut curry reduction; curry paste is chilli and aromatics with no wheat, but shrimp paste and fish sauce are standard. Fried white fish version ¥940.

items.ja: パネーンムー / 豚ばら肉の濃厚カレー炒め
items.en: Pork belly in a rich panang curry
items.note: Panang is curry paste, coconut cream and kaffir lime — no flour. Fish sauce and shrimp paste.

items.ja: パットマーマー / 即席めんの炒め物
items.en: Stir-fried instant noodles — the shop calls it Thai B-grade gourmet
items.note: The shop names the noodle: インスタント麺, instant noodles, which are WHEAT. On a menu where most noodles are rice, this is the one that is not.

items.ja: パットウンセン / 焼き春雨の香ばし炒め
items.en: Stir-fried glass noodles — the shop recommends it to people who dislike heat
items.note: The noodle is fine — 春雨 is mung bean starch — and the shop rules the dish out in its own description: タイ醤油味, THAI SOY SAUCE. Named by the kitchen rather than inferred.

items.ja: パットゥアンゴーク / 豚ばら肉ともやしのオイスターソース炒め
items.en: Pork belly and bean sprouts in oyster sauce — the shop calls it a Thai mother's dish
items.note: Stir-fried with OYSTER SAUCE, which the shop names in its own English — a wheat route and an animal one at once.

items.ja: パットパックルアミット / いろどり野菜炒め
items.note: An all-vegetable dish that is out on both axes for one reason: the shop's own English names OYSTER SAUCE. Stir-fried with OYSTER SAUCE, which the shop names in its own English — a wheat route and an animal one at once. Worth asking whether it can be made without.

items.ja: ガイパットメットマムアン / 鶏肉とカシューナッツの炒め物
items.note: Cashew chicken is built on oyster sauce and soy, and the chicken is normally floured before frying.

items.ja: パットトーミョー / 豆苗のファイヤー炒め
items.en: Fired pea shoots — the shop calls it a simple dish for drinking
items.note: The simplest stir-fry on the board — greens and garlic over high heat. Thai greens are normally finished with oyster or soy sauce, so ask for garlic and salt only; this is the one most likely to be granted.

items.en: Tom yum kung, for two to three
items.note: Lemongrass, galangal, lime and chilli with no wheat in the classic build. Fish sauce and prawn.

items.ja: トムカーガイ / 鶏肉のココナッツミルクスープ（2〜3名様分）
items.en: Coconut and lemongrass chicken soup, for two to three
items.note: Coconut, galangal and lime with no wheat route. Fish sauce and chicken.

items.ja: ゲンチューウンセン / 春雨と豆腐のあっさりスープ（2〜3名様分）
items.en: Clear glass noodle and tofu soup — the shop notes it is neither hot nor sour
items.note: Genuinely worth asking about: glass noodles and tofu are both plant and neither is wheat, and the shop describes it as gentle rather than chilli-based. What is undeclared is the broth, which in a Thai gaeng jued is normally pork stock, and any fish sauce.

items.ja: ゲンキョーワーン / 鶏肉と茄子のグリーンカレー（2〜3名様分）
items.en: Green curry with chicken and aubergine, jasmine rice included, for two to three
items.note: A strong coeliac prospect: curry paste and coconut milk over rice, with no flour roux and no bread. Green curry paste conventionally contains shrimp paste and the dish is finished with fish sauce. Thai cooking is built on ナンプラー (fish sauce) and frequently shrimp paste, so a dish with no visible meat is still rarely vegan without asking.

items.ja: ゲーンチェンマイ / 豚肉と野菜のチェンマイカレー（2〜3名様分）
items.en: Chiang Mai curry with pork and vegetables, jasmine rice included — the shop recommends it to people who dislike heat
items.note: Northern Thai curries are water- rather than coconut-based; no wheat route. Thai cooking is built on ナンプラー (fish sauce) and frequently shrimp paste, so a dish with no visible meat is still rarely vegan without asking.
Rice-based; Thai fried rice is seasoned with fish sauce and often soy. Prawn version also listed.

items.en: Thai sticky rice — the shop suggests eating it with the salads, Thai style
items.note: Steamed glutinous rice. Worth saying plainly because the English name misleads: "glutinous" describes the sticky texture and contains NO GLUTEN. Rice and water, and the safest order here.

items.ja: パッキーマオ / タイ太米麺酔っ払い焼きそば
items.en: Drunken noodles with wide rice noodles — the shop explains the name comes from adding too much chilli while drunk
items.note: The shop names the noodle 米麺 — RICE — so the noodle is fine. Pad kee mao is built on soy and oyster sauce, which is not.

items.ja: パッタイ / タイ焼きそば
items.en: Pad thai — stir-fried in a sauce of simmered tamarind and red onion, lightly sweet
items.note: The noodle is rice and the shop describes the sauce as tamarind and red onion rather than soy, which is more promising than most pad thai entries in this dataset. Fish sauce is still standard, and the dish normally contains egg, dried shrimp and peanut. Worth asking.

items.ja: レックトム / トムヤムラーメン
items.note: Despite ラーメン in the Japanese name, レック is a thin RICE noodle — the shop calls its noodles 米麺 throughout this section. The tom yum broth is fish- and shrimp-based.

items.ja: レックナーム / あっさり鶏肉ヌードル
items.en: Clear chicken noodle soup — the shop notes Thai rice noodles suit the light broth
items.note: The shop states タイの米麺 — RICE noodles — in its own description. The broth is chicken and normally seasoned with fish sauce.

items.ja: パットシーユー / タイ太麺焼きそば
items.en: Wide rice noodle stir-fry — the shop notes it suits people who dislike heat
items.note: The shop names the noodle as タイの太い米麺, rice — and the dish name names what rules it out: ผัดซีอิ๊ว means "fried with SOY SAUCE". A rice noodle in a wheat sauce.

items.ja: カノムモーゲン / タロイモ焼きプリン
items.en: Baked taro pudding made with taro and coconut milk
items.note: Taro and coconut milk, baked — the classic recipe is set with EGG and uses mung bean or rice flour, both gluten-free. Egg rules out vegan. Coconut or mango ice topping +¥100.

items.ja: カノムトゥアイ / ココナッツミルクと米粉のもちもちデザート
items.en: Bite-size coconut and rice-flour mochi sweets
items.note: ⚠ THE SHOP NAMES THE FLOUR: 「ココナッツミルクと米粉を使った」 — coconut milk and RICE FLOUR. Both plant, neither wheat, stated by the kitchen rather than inferred. The best dessert on this board for both diets at once, and the reason to read the descriptions here.

items.ja: サクー / タピオカココナッツミルク
items.note: Tapioca is CASSAVA starch and coconut milk is plant — no wheat and no dairy in the classic build, and the cheapest dessert here. Coconut ice or mango sorbet topping +¥100.

items.ja: アイティムカティ / ココナッツアイス
items.en: Coconut ice cream — the shop describes it as clean rather than over-sweet
items.note: Thai coconut ice cream is traditionally made with coconut milk rather than dairy, which would make it vegan as well as wheat-free — and this shop's framing suggests the coconut version rather than a cream one. Nothing is declared, so ask.

items.ja: アイティムマムアン / マンゴーソルベ
items.en: Mango sorbet with fruit pulp, lightly frozen
items.note: A sorbet is fruit, sugar and water in its classic form, which would suit both diets; the shop describes real mango pulp. Nothing is declared.

tokyo_tanaka_sobaten_asakusa.price_note: ⚠⚠ THE MOST IMPORTANT THING THIS SHOP PUBLISHES IS A WARNING, NOT A MENU. Its parent company issues a per-dish allergen table covering the 8 statutory allergens and the 20 recommended ones, and the table opens by saying the kitchen CANNOT exclude allergens: 「当店の厨房設備及び商品の製造上、アレルギー食材を完全に除くことができません」. THE SHOP ASKS PEOPLE WITH SEVERE ALLERGIES NOT TO EAT HERE, in its own words: 「ごく微量でも発症する症状をお持ちの場合は、田中そば店でのお食事を取りやめて頂きますようお願い申し上げます」 — if you react to trace amounts, please do not dine with us. It also states it may refuse service outright. It further discloses that all dishes share cooking equipment (「各メニューの調理には同じ調理器具を使用しているため、本来その商品に使用しない食材が調理時に付着・混入する可能性があります」) and that the factory making its noodles and soups also produces items containing 小麦、卵、乳成分. tokyo_rice_hack_gluten_free_ba.price_note: ⚠ THIS IS A DEDICATED GLUTEN-FREE BAKERY AND THE RARE CASE WHERE THE ANSWER IS YES. Every product is made with 米粉 — RICE FLOUR — and natural yeast, and the shop says so throughout its own copy rather than leaving it to be inferred: the curry filling is 「もちろんグルテンフリー」, the pizza is 「完全グルテンフリー」, and the parent company (株式会社ライステラス) presents itself as a gluten-free café, bakery and cooking school. Set that beside the ベーカリー サンチノ record in this dataset — a 米粉パン専門店 that turns out to add 10% vital wheat gluten — and the difference is that this shop states the claim and that one never did. ⚠ TWO HONEST LIMITS. First, no Japanese gluten-free CERTIFICATION exists and none is claimed here; this rests on the shop's own word, which is how every GF claim in Japan works. Second, I found no explicit statement that the premises handle no wheat at all — the claim is about the products, not audited about the building — so a highly sensitive coeliac still has one question to ask. ⚠ SEASONAL: the shop states 「夏季はバゲット・マフィン・ピザ・ホットドッグのみの販売となります」 — in summer only baguettes, muffins, pizza and hot dogs are sold, so the bread and curry buns below may not be available. Muffins and hot dogs are named in that line but carry no published price and are not listed as items. 神宮前5-16-5; closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

tokyo_thali_ya_shibuya_namikib.price_note: No menu found, and it was chased properly before giving up. The branch page carries address, hours and seating but no dishes; the chain homepage links no menu page; the Tabelog menu page carries nothing; and the one PDF the chain does publish (2023.pdf) turns out to be a NEW YEAR TRADING SCHEDULE for its branches rather than a menu — and its text is CID-encoded mojibake at that. So the empty list is the honest answer. ⚠ WHAT IS ESTABLISHED, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: the branch page states 「ハラールフレンドリー対象店舗です」 — halal-friendly. That is a real dietary designation but NOT the one this app tracks: halal-friendly means no pork and no alcohol, and says nothing whatever about wheat, dairy or egg. A halal kitchen is not a vegan or gluten-free one. ⚠ THE STRUCTURAL POINT FOR A COELIAC, established elsewhere in this dataset at SAPANA and worth carrying here: at an Indian restaurant the CURRY is usually the safe half and THE BREAD IS THE PROBLEM. Indian curries are built on onion, tomato and ground spice rather than the flour roux a Japanese カレー uses, so a curry with RICE is a different proposition from the same curry with ナン — and naan is wheat bread, full stop. This chain's name is インド定食ターリー屋 and a thali is a rice-centred plate, so the swap is likely to be easy to ask for. 36 seats, open year-round, 11:00–23:00.

tokyo_cafe_trois_bagues.price_note: No menu published. The café's own site is a single page about its history and its coffee with no dish, no drink list and no price on it, and the Tabelog menu page carries nothing. ⚠ WHAT THE SITE DOES ESTABLISH, and it is all about the coffee: this is a small 喫茶店 opened in 1976 (昭和51年) that ages green beans before roasting them — エイジングコーヒー, old beans — and brews them by NEL DRIP, the flannel-cloth method. That matters more than it sounds for both diets, because it is the one preparation detail that could carry something: a nel filter is cloth rather than paper, reused and hand-washed, so the question of what else has passed through it is at least askable, though coffee itself has no wheat route. The site also states it stocks wine and beer — ⚠ BEER IS BARLEY, and 大麦 is not on Japan's statutory allergen list, so nothing will ever flag it. Black coffee itself is gluten-free and vegan; the milk in anything else is not, and no plant milk is mentioned anywhere. NOTHING IS RECORDED ABOUT THE FOOD because the shop publishes nothing about it. 神田神保町1-12-1 富田ビルB1, one minute from Jimbocho A5; closed Sundays.

tokyo_shichiten_hakki.price_note: No prices and no dish names: the shop's own site shows its お品書き as images grouped under ラーメン, つけ麺, トッピング, サイド and ドリンク, with nothing readable in text, and the Tabelog menu page carries nothing. That makes this the FOURTH shop in shard s14 alone whose menu is published only as pictures — a pattern worth naming, because it is not a shop declining to publish, it is a menu that exists and cannot be machine-read. ⚠ WHAT THE SITE DOES STATE IS THE NOODLE, AND IT IS THE ANSWER: 「三河屋製麺特注のストレート極太麺」 — custom-made extra-thick straight noodles from MIKAWAYA SEIMEN, a noodle maker. A ramen noodle from a Japanese seimen-jo is wheat; a shop naming its supplier is signalling quality, not composition. The broth is 鶏・豚・魚介のトリプルスープ — chicken, pork and seafood — which rules out vegan three times over and, being a ramen tare, will be soy-seasoned as well. tokyo_pan_ya_nishi_shinjuku.price_note: No menu found. The record's stored website is an X (Twitter) account, which is not a menu this dataset can cite, and the Tabelog menu page carries nothing. ⚠ THE CATEGORY ANSWER IS THE RECORD HERE, and it needs saying because the descriptor invites a misreading: this is a 天然酵母パン bakery — NATURAL-YEAST bread. 天然酵母 describes the LEAVENING, not the flour. A naturally leavened loaf is still a wheat loaf unless the bakery says otherwise, and nothing here says otherwise. It is worth flagging explicitly because 天然酵母, 全粒粉 and 米粉 all read as "healthier bread" to a casual eye and only one of them is gluten-free — and this dataset has already met a 米粉パン専門店 (ベーカリー サンチノ) that added 10% vital wheat gluten anyway. A coeliac should assume wheat at a Japanese bakery unless the shop makes the claim the way RICE HACK does. Vegan is a separate open question: naturally leavened bread is often just flour, water, salt and starter, but Japanese bakeries commonly enrich with milk, butter and egg.

tokyo_hommage.price_note: PARTIAL BY THE NATURE OF THE RESTAURANT, not by a gap in the research: this is a two-Michelin-star gastronomic restaurant in Asakusa and it sells COURSES, not dishes — the site publishes course prices and no menu, and the Tabelog menu page carries nothing. So there are prices below and no dish names, which is the correct shape for this record. ⚠ PRICES ARE 税込サービス料10%別 — tax included but a 10% SERVICE CHARGE is added on top, which the shop states plainly and which most records in this dataset do not have. ⚠ THE SITE CARRIES UNDATED AND PROBABLY STALE CONTENT: its anniversary note reads 17周年 and its Michelin line refers to the 2018 guide, and there is a separate Christmas and New Year block with weekday-dates that do not match the current year. The standing lunch and dinner prices below are the ones presented as the regular menu; the seasonal block is not recorded. No allergen statement anywhere. Also offered: a French おせち for New Year at ¥80,000 for a two-tier box, with pâté de campagne at ¥16,000 full size and ¥8,000 half.

items.en: Lunch course — the shop lists three price points; served Monday and Tuesday, and Wednesday and Thursday lunch
items.note: Three lunch courses at ¥16,000, ¥28,000 and ¥38,500, all 税込サービス料10%別. A gastronomic tasting menu, so the dishes are the chef's and change constantly — none is published and none is invented here. ⚠ FRENCH FINE DINING IS THE ONE FORMAT IN THIS DATASET WHERE ASKING IN ADVANCE USUALLY WORKS. The structural wheat is real — bread service, flour-thickened sauces, pastry desserts — but a kitchen at this level normally adapts a menu with notice, unlike a ramen counter or a set teishoku where nothing can be changed. The conversation belongs at the reservation, not the table.

Two dinner courses at ¥28,000 and ¥38,500, both 税込サービス料10%別. A gastronomic tasting menu, so the dishes are the chef's and change constantly — none is published and none is invented here. ⚠ FRENCH FINE DINING IS THE ONE FORMAT IN THIS DATASET WHERE ASKING IN ADVANCE USUALLY WORKS. The structural wheat is real — bread service, flour-thickened sauces, pastry desserts — but a kitchen at this level normally adapts a menu with notice, unlike a ramen counter or a set teishoku where nothing can be changed. tokyo_shin_chan_ramen.price_note: No menu published: the shop's own page carries a single link to a Gnavi menu and lists no dish and no price of its own, and the Tabelog menu page carries nothing. ⚠ THE ONE PRODUCTION DETAIL THE SHOP DOES PUBLISH IS THE NOODLE, AND IT IS THE ANSWER: 「麺は自家製麺を使用！」 — the noodles are made in house. A shop making its own ramen noodles is telling you about craft, not composition: a 自家製麺 at a ramen shop is wheat, and making it on the premises means wheat flour is worked in the same room as everything else. The same line adds 「スープは炊きたてなみなみで！チャーシューは切りたて」 — freshly boiled soup and freshly cut chashu, and chashu is braised in soy sauce. 15 seats, so a small counter with no room to keep anything separate. 新宿4-2-7, one minute from Shinjuku-sanchome.

tokyo_sakana_ryo_ri_nojima.price_note: No menu found and nothing else either. The Tabelog menu page carries no items, the listing page yields no structured shop data or visitor accounts that could be read, and the record's stored website is the Tabelog listing itself — the shop has no site of its own. That leaves nothing citable, so the empty list is the honest answer rather than an unfinished one. ⚠ WHAT THE CATEGORY IMPLIES, offered as orientation rather than as findings about this shop: a 魚料理 house is fish and rice, which starts better than most for a coeliac because sashimi and rice carry no wheat. What does is everything around them — the soy sauce sashimi is dipped in, any 煮付け (simmered in soy and mirin), any 西京漬け (miso, potentially 麦味噌 and therefore barley), the tempura or kara-age if there is a fried section, and the miso soup that comes with a set. Nothing here suits a vegan. None of that is recorded as items because none of it is sourced for this restaurant.
